newsitem.title: USA: U.S. January PPI evinces no inflation signs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. January PPI evinces no inflation signs.

text.p: The January U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI) delivered a Valentine's Day gift to the credit markets on Friday, showing no material inflation pressures anywhere in the economy, a situation that should allow the Federal Reserve to keep monetary policy on hold, economists said.

The government unexpectedly reported the PPI fell by 0.3 percent in January. The PPI without its more volatile food and energy components was unchanged. A 0.3 percent rise in the index and a 0.2 percent gain in the core had been forecast.

"We didn't expect a big drop in the headline number and it was just all around a good report," said Sandy Batten, international economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A. "We had declines in energy and food prices and the rest of the price components were unchanged."
Batten said the data mean the Fed will remain on hold.

"The Fed has the same situation they've had for the last eight or 10 months," said Batten. "The employment picture is tight and generates some anxiety for them. But at the same time, they can't put their finger on inflation pressures anywhere else in the economy."
The bond augmented opening gains after seeing the favorable price report. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 14/32 to 101-5/32, yielding 6.54 percent, half an hour after the PPI came out.
"The report was pretty favorable," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
"We were surprised by the drop in the total index, but energy prices are dropping, (putting downward pressure on the overall inflation measure)," he said.
"On a year-over-year basis, you need a microscope to see inflation in the goods sector," said Glassman.
